Given the current growth of data centers and the grid constraints, it is very important to understand how data center design and operations interact with the grid and what types of grid disturbances/events a data center can “ride-through” and assist the grid during instability events. In recent times, there is a lot of attention on developing data centers as a flexible load on the grid using a variety of approaches, such as on-site generation, on-site energy storage, and compute job scheduling, and by dispatching cooling systems. As noted, every system architecture shown inFigure 1 has generators except that from Verrus, which also has BESS (Figure 1 (f)). A comparison of the effectiveness of these different approaches for data center load flexibility is discussed in a recent report from EPRI (2025). From the grid operator’s perspective, it is important to be able to better understand how such components of the data center power system could be leveraged to improve grid reliability. The next section describes a model of individual components that need to be integrated to develop an EMT domain model of any of the data center power system architectures shown in Figure 1. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Modeling Framework Overview The modeling framework builds on high-fidelity EMT representations developed through offline simulations and validated in real-time CHIL environments. To ensure the reliable and scalable integration of data centers into the grid, a flexible and detailed modeling approach is required. The framework should support: • Offline EMT simulations—comprehensive time domain models using tools like PSCAD for detailed disturbance studies • Real-time EMT simulations—CHIL environments enabling closed-loop control and dynamic studies, including actual devices and controllers. 8 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3 System Modeling Layers 3.1 Utility Interface and Medium-Voltage Bus An accurate model of the utility interface must: • Model the data center POI as a dynamic, voltage-/frequency-sensitive node, parameterized with a realistic grid impedance (resistance and reactance) to simulate both strong and weak utility grid (e.g., N-1 contingency) scenarios. • Incorporate medium-voltage protection relays and utility coordination schemes to ensure reliable fault detection and grid compliance. • Simulate voltage sag/swells, frequency excursions, and POI oscillations, including those driven by rapid changes in AI loads. 3.1.1 Standard PSCAD Models Available The PSCAD standard library includes: • Three-phase medium-voltage bus and basic node models • Standard relays (overcurrent/undervoltage) • Circuit breakers and line elements • Modules for simulating common voltage/frequency disturbances. 3.1.2 Additional Model Requirements Custom or advanced model enhancements might be required to: • Parameterize the grid impedance at the POI to reflect the dynamic strength of the grid, enabling accurate representation of strong (high short-circuit ratio) and weak (low short- circuit ratio) grid behaviors and their effects on system stability and control interactions (Shah 2024). • Implement
